I’ll read the repository guidance and the project’s overview, then begin the research and record the results, progress, and chat history in the project folder.

The program’s first milestone is a bounded certificate with a fair comparison against direct jet exclusion. I’m checking the existing theta estimates and collision controls so the first calculation can establish a concrete margin or identify precisely where the proposed method loses.

I found an important limit to the simplest approach: a constant reference map gives the same exclusion bound as direct evaluation, by the maximum principle. I’ll use a nonconstant reference around a small complex-time neighborhood of a theta zero and compare both methods using the same source errors. I’m also using the writing skill to keep the notes and progress record in the repository’s established format.

The pilot has a positive bound on a smooth domain with complex heat-time radius \(0.01\) and spatial radius \(0.125\), centered at \(z=28.25\). It gives zero relative charge, but direct derivative exclusion gives a stronger margin using fewer source integrals. On the same-sized domain, the quadratic collision control gives charge one, so the method correctly retains a genuine collision.

The first comparison is complete. The charge certificate has a gap above \(7.495\times10^{-5}\); direct derivative exclusion improves that to \(7.993\times10^{-5}\) with six source integrals instead of eight. I’m saving the derivation, replayable calculation, and self-review, and marking the global coverage questions as open.

Completed the first bounded research pilot.

It certifies zero relative charge near a real theta zero, with margin above **0.00007495**. Direct derivative exclusion performs better: margin above **0.00007993**, using six source integrals instead of eight. The quadratic collision control correctly returns charge one.

I’ll continue with a domain containing two neighboring zeros and their intervening stationary point, then compare the boundary-charge certificate with direct joint-jet exclusion using the same data.

A structural check changes the next step: for a holomorphic reference pair with no common zero, its minimum norm is already attained on the boundary. I’m verifying this carefully. If it applies here, moving from one zero to two would still give direct joint exclusion the same certified margin, so a larger theta calculation would not establish an advantage by itself.

The structural result holds for the proposed holomorphic references: their boundary margin already gives the same lower bound throughout the domain. I’ve also checked a boundary-only degree method on exact models, including two zeros separated by a stationary point. I’m documenting the proof, the controls, and what remains to test on the full theta kernel.

The boundary-only controls give the expected charges: zero for the two-root model and one for the collision model. A separate orientation check also passes. These calculations bound the error across every boundary simplex, not just at sample points. They validate the method, but a theta-specific cost advantage is still untested.

The new note now contains the transfer proof, a sharp heat-model example, and the exact boundary-degree checks. I’m updating the progress register to separate those completed results from the remaining theta experiment, while preserving the first pilot and its cheaper direct comparison.

The continuation is saved, and all four exact controls passed with the expected charges. The next step is recorded: estimate whether a complete theta boundary calculation can pay its interpolation error before running a large grid. No theta advantage or global simplicity result is claimed from this round.

I’ll test whether the boundary method is practical for the complete theta field on a domain containing two neighboring zeros. The exact controls support the method’s correctness; this next comparison will show whether it offers a useful computational advantage.

The preliminary values support a concrete test box: real position 28–43, with small widths in complex time and imaginary position. I’ll certify that it contains two neighboring real zeros and compare the boundary calculation with direct interpolation using the same data. This thin-box layout lets both methods reuse the boundary vertices, which may limit the advantage.

I’ve fixed the test budget: 1,032 validated source integrals, 2,056 boundary vertices and 9,228 boundary tetrahedra. The direct comparison will reuse those vertices across 256 interior cells. Both calculations will include all omitted source terms and interpolation errors, so their margins and costs can be compared fairly.

The complete-theta test passed: it certifies zero charge on the box and exactly two neighboring real zeros with one stationary point between them. The comparison is less encouraging for a speed advantage: direct interpolation uses the same boundary data, gives a stronger margin, and takes less computation. I’m saving that result with its limits.

The source audit now confirms that every field anchor is on the outer boundary. The notes include the full error bounds and the root-count proof. I’m updating the register to mark this finite comparison complete and to make any further experiment justify a different cost advantage before expanding the computation.

The full-theta test succeeded: it certifies zero charge on a box containing two neighboring simple zeros and their intervening stationary point.

The comparison tempers the optimism: **direct exclusion uses the same data, gives a roughly 10% stronger margin, and requires less computation.** The boundary method works, but this experiment establishes no advantage.

Saved [Note 03](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-3/13_contradiction_analysis/04_boundary_winding/threshold_routes/12_relative_chern_hopf_charges/notes/03_TWO_ZERO_THETA_BOUNDARY_AND_DIRECT_COMPARISON_20261021.md), the replayable calculation and self-review, and updated progress and chat records. The next research gate is to identify a domain or acquisition method with a credible cost advantage.

Let's think about this more abstractly and analytically than numerically. Does this show that this method is not competitive, or just that it doesn't compete numerically? What can be gained here potentially?

I’ll separate the mathematical limitation from the measured cost result, then examine what the charge formulation could still offer analytically. I’ll record that assessment in the research notes and progress register.

The numerical result is narrower than a verdict on the method. There is also a genuine analytic limitation: a particular holomorphic-reference argument gives the same exclusion bound as direct analysis. But that does not rule out using the charge as a global integer constrained by an identity, deformation, or conservation law. That distinction is where the next research should focus.

A useful analytic payoff is that each collision contributes a positive integer, while simple zeros contribute nothing. An independently derived upper bound below one would therefore exclude every collision in a region without locating them individually.

I’m also making the connection to the discriminant explicit: when a finite group of zeros stays inside a fixed spatial contour, its total charge becomes the winding number of one holomorphic function of heat time. That gives us a concrete analytic object to study; it does not yet supply the bound needed for theta.

The distinction is clearer now: the method could be useful analytically even if it remains slower as a numerical certificate. Its potential is to control a whole collection of collisions through one invariant.

There is also a useful limit on that hope. The theta function’s usual reflection and reality symmetries preserve the charge; they do not force it to vanish. Any decisive argument will need more than those symmetries—such as an estimate using the actual theta source.

I’ve recorded the analytical assessment and revised the next research step. It now asks for a theta-specific bound or identity that controls the charge, rather than requiring a numerical speed advantage. The earlier benchmark conclusions remain intact.

The new note also explains why this remains difficult: rewriting the charge through a discriminant retains the collision singularity and the influence of the other zeros. The reformulation gives us a clearer target, but the decisive estimate is still missing.

**The results do not show that this method is analytically uncompetitive.** They establish numerical losses for two implementations, plus an analytic limitation for one particular mechanism. My previous recommendation made computational competitiveness too central.

The analytic limitation is substantive: if we start with a known degree-zero holomorphic reference, boundary floor \(b\), and approximation error \(e<b\), then direct analysis already gives the same interior floor \(b-e\). Repackaging that certificate as a charge calculation supplies no stronger conclusion. But an independent way of determining the charge could have considerable value.

The main potential is to turn many local separation problems into **one global integer constraint**. For a bounded region with nonzero boundary jet,
\[
Q_B=\sum_{\text{collision events }p}\binom{m_p}{2}
\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.
\]
Simple zeros contribute nothing; double events contribute one; triple events contribute three. Consequently:

- An independently derived bound \(Q_B<1\) excludes every collision in the region.
- A weaker bound \(Q_B<3\) already excludes triple and higher events.
- A bound on total charge could constrain many events without locating them individually.

The substantive challenge is deriving that bound. Integrality makes a suitable estimate powerful; it does not provide the estimate.

There are two further potential gains. First, a signed boundary identity might retain correlations and cancellations that our pointwise absolute-value estimates discard. The individual collision charges remain positive, so any cancellation occurs in the boundary expression. Second, an explicit deformation to a configuration of known charge could determine the answer without requiring uniform closeness to one reference. Degree is invariant throughout a deformation that avoids zero on the boundary. [Hatcher’s account of degree](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch2.pdf) supplies the standard topological foundation.

I worked out a more concrete analytic connection. Suppose a finite group of spatial zeros remains inside a fixed contour as complex heat time varies, with no collision on the time boundary. Form its monic polynomial \(P(t,z)\) and discriminant
\[
\Delta(t)=\operatorname{Disc}_z P(t,z).
\]
Then
\[
Q_B=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint\frac{\Delta'(t)}{\Delta(t)}\,dt.
\]
Thus the charge becomes the winding number of **one holomorphic function of heat time**. This extends the existing local discriminant interpretation to a finite cluster. It gives us a specific object on which to seek analytic identities, factorization, or bounds on its argument. It also avoids choosing and tracking individual root labels.

The remaining difficulty is real. The usual reality and parity symmetries preserve charge rather than force it to vanish. And the elementary heat solution \(H=z^2-2t\) has \(\Delta(t)=8t\): its roots are simple for every positive real time, yet an endpoint collision remains. Positivity at positive time therefore cannot finish the argument.

**I would continue analytically**, with the target of an estimate using the complete theta source that restricts this winding or total charge. That could be valuable even if the resulting numerical certificate stayed slower. We have a useful invariant and a clearer analytic formulation; we do not yet have the theta-specific estimate that makes it decisive.

Please continue analytically as described

I’ll pursue the discriminant formulation analytically, focusing on what the complete theta source can say about its winding. I’ll first check the existing endpoint estimates, then work toward a precise bound or identify the term that prevents one, and record the result in the notes and progress register.

The two-zero case has a useful simplification. Its discriminant satisfies a first-order equation with a fixed forcing term, while the influence of all other zeros sits in one analytic coefficient. I’m checking whether controlling that coefficient can bound the number of collisions in a complex-time region without assuming a lower bound on the gap between the two zeros.

The calculation now gives a conditional analytic result: if the two zeros stay isolated from the others, and the exterior coefficient varies slowly enough across the imaginary-time width, their discriminant can vanish at most once. Reality symmetry then forces that collision to occur at real time.

Under those conditions, the full complex charge is determined by two real endpoint signs. I’m checking how to bound the exterior coefficient from complete-source data and making the remaining endpoint obstruction explicit.

The proof gives an explicit admissible width for the complex-time strip, using complete theta moments and lower bounds on the spatial boundary. That width does not divide by the internal root gap, so it can remain positive even when the two roots collide.

The limitation is now precise: this controls the possible collisions, but excluding a time-zero collision still requires an independent signed endpoint estimate. The quadratic collision model passes the new bounds and correctly returns charge one.

The exact controls agree with the formula: matching endpoint signs give charge zero, and a negative-to-positive change gives charge one. A second algebraic derivation also confirms the constant in the discriminant equation without tracking individual roots.

I’m saving this as a conditional analytic theorem. The notes clearly separate it from the still-unproved theta boundary bounds and endpoint signs needed for an exclusion result.

I’ve proved a **conditional analytic reduction for an isolated pair of zeros**, recorded in [Note 05](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-3/13_contradiction_analysis/04_boundary_winding/threshold_routes/12_relative_chern_hopf_charges/notes/05_TWO_ROOT_DISCRIMINANT_FLOW_AND_REAL_CAP_CHARGE_20261021.md).

Their discriminant—the squared separation—satisfies
\[
\Delta'(t)=8+A(t)\Delta(t),
\]
where \(A\) is analytic and can be bounded from a spatial contour **without dividing by the gap between the two roots**. It remains regular even when they collide.

For a real-symmetric time window, if \(|A|\le K\) and its imaginary-time half-width satisfies \(K\tau<\pi/2\), a [standard univalence argument](https://www.numdam.org/item/10.1016/j.crma.2018.02.007.pdf) gives:

- At most one collision in the entire complex-time window.
- Any collision must have real time and position.
- With nonzero endpoint discriminants, matching signs give charge zero; negative followed by positive gives charge one.

I also derived an explicit sufficient strip width using complete theta moments and independently proved spatial-boundary lower bounds.

The analytic gain is that we can control complex collision events while allowing the internal gap to close. **The remaining obstacle is the signed endpoint estimate:** the phase bound alone permits a collision. The quadratic control correctly returns charge one, and no new theta region has yet had all these hypotheses established.
